title: Food Markets in Europe: Buy, Eat, Pay and Tip
summary: Food markets can be open-air, covered, or inside food halls. A few clear questions help you choose food, check allergens, pay, and handle tips.

cover.alt: Shoppers chat with a market seller beside displays of bread, cheese, fruit, olives, and prepared food at a sunny European market.

blocks.title: A Simple Plan for the Market
paragraphs: Food markets can be open-air, covered, or inside food halls. A few clear questions help you choose food, check allergens, pay, and handle tips.

items.prompt: What food do you like to buy at a market?
items.explanation: You can name fruit, bread, cheese, a snack, or another food.

items.prompt: Do you prefer to pay by card or in cash? Why?
items.explanation: There is no single correct answer. Think about what is easy for you.

items.prompt: When do you usually leave a tip?
items.explanation: Think about cafés, restaurants, counters, and table service.

blocks.title: Three Kinds of Food Market
paragraphs: Buying food at European food markets becomes easier when you know the basic layout. An open-air market has stalls outside. A covered market puts the stalls under one roof. A food hall is usually inside and often has places to sit. Any of these places may sell ingredients, ready-to-eat dishes, or both. Picture fruit in Barcelona, a warm lunch in Paris, and bread in London. First, walk around and look at the displayed price. Notice whether people order at a counter or sit at a table. These details help you know how to buy, eat, and pay. Local market cultures differ, so watch first and ask politely when you are unsure.

items.prompt: What two details can help you understand how to use a new food market?
items.answer: Look at the displayed price and notice whether people order at a counter or sit at a table.
items.explanation: These details help you understand how people buy, eat, and pay there.

blocks.title: Choose an Amount and Ask How to Pay
paragraphs: Food may be sold by piece or by weight. For one bread roll, say, “Two of these, please,” and point. For a practice cheese order, say, “Half a kilo, please,” or ask for a smaller amount. The seller can stop when you say, “That’s enough, thank you.” You can also ask what is local or popular. Ask for a small sample only when it seems possible; the seller may say yes or no. Before the seller prepares the order, check payment with “Do you take cards?” or “Is it cash only?” This avoids a problem after the food is ready.

items.prompt: What can you ask before a seller prepares your order?
items.answer: You can ask whether the stall takes cards or is cash only.
items.explanation: Checking first helps you avoid a payment problem after the food is ready.

rows.meaning: Ask the seller for a popular choice.
Ask whether the food comes from the area.

rows.example: Half a kilo of tomatoes, please.

rows.meaning: Ask whether you can pay by card.
rows.example: Do you take cards, or is it cash only?

blocks.title: Ask Clearly About Allergens
paragraphs: Allergies need clear questions. In the European Union, fourteen allergens are regulated. Sellers of non-prepacked food, including food at restaurant and deli counters, must provide allergen information. They may explain it aloud, and written information must be available on request. This helps, but it is not a promise that cross-contact cannot happen. A little of another food may touch the dish during preparation. Say exactly what you cannot eat, ask to see the written information, and listen to the answer. If the answer is not safe or clear enough for you, choose something else. Never guess about a serious allergy.

items.prompt: Why should a traveller still ask clearly after reading allergen information?
items.answer: Because allergen information does not guarantee that cross-contact cannot happen.
items.explanation: The traveller should explain the allergy and choose another item if the answer is not safe or clear enough.

rows.meaning: Ask whether nuts are an ingredient.
rows.example: Does this contain nuts or sesame?
I am allergic to nuts, so I need to be careful.

rows.term: Can I see the written information?
rows.meaning: Ask to read the allergen details.
rows.example: Can I see the written information, please?

blocks.title: Tips Depend on the Country and Service
paragraphs: Tipping is not one European rule. In Spain, restaurant tips are discretionary. At a tapas bar, a customer may round up the bill; at a higher-end restaurant, about 10% can be used. In France, service compris means that service is included, so an extra tip is optional. In Britain, a bill can name a discretionary or compulsory service charge. Read the words on the bill before you decide. Also ask what kind of service you received. At a simple counter, pay the stated price unless local information suggests something different. At a table, check the bill and the local custom before adding more money.

items.prompt: What should you check before adding a tip at a table?
items.answer: Check the bill, the kind of service, and the local custom before adding more money.
items.explanation: Tipping rules differ, and the bill may already name a service charge.

rows.meaning: Ask whether service is already in the price.
Ask whether the bill adds money for service.
rows.example: Is there a service charge on this bill?

rows.term: Do I need to leave a tip?
rows.meaning: Ask whether an extra tip is normal.
rows.example: Do I need to leave a tip as well?

rows.term: I will pay the stated price.
rows.meaning: Say that you will pay the shown amount.
rows.example: Thank you. I will pay the stated price.

blocks.title: Scene 1: A Market Stall in Barcelona
paragraphs: This is a fictional practice stall in Barcelona, Spain. The seller has local tomatoes and accepts card payment in this exercise. In Spain, restaurant tips are discretionary, and a customer at a tapas bar may round up the bill.
Your goal is to ask what is local, order two items, check card payment, and decide whether to tip.

images.alt: An adult traveller points to tomatoes while a market seller holds out a card terminal at a Barcelona produce stall.

blocks.title: Roleplay: Choose and Pay in Barcelona

turns.speaker: Seller
turns.text: Hello! What would you like?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: What is local and popular here?

turns.speaker: Seller
turns.text: The tomatoes are local and popular in this practice stall.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Great. Two of these, please. Do you take cards?

turns.speaker: Seller
turns.text: Yes, this fictional stall takes cards.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Do I need to leave a tip?

turns.speaker: Seller
turns.text: In Spain, a tip is your choice. At a casual tapas bar, some customers simply round up.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I will pay the stated price today. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Seller
turns.text: Thank you. Your two tomatoes are ready.

blocks.title: Scene 2: A Food Counter in Paris
paragraphs: This is a fictional prepared-food counter in a covered market in Paris, France. An allergen card is available for the non-prepacked dishes. Under European Union rules, the seller may also explain the information aloud, but the card cannot promise that cross-contact never happens.
Your goal is to ask about nuts, read the allergen information, and make a safe personal choice.

images.alt: An adult traveller listens as a cook points to allergen symbols at a prepared-food counter in a covered Paris market.

blocks.title: Roleplay: Ask About Allergens in Paris

turns.speaker: Cook
turns.text: Hello. Would you like the lentil salad?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: What is in it? I am allergic to nuts.

turns.speaker: Cook
turns.text: The written allergen card says it contains almonds. Cross-contact is also possible.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Thank you for telling me. Can I see the written information?

turns.speaker: Cook
turns.text: Yes. European Union rules allow a spoken answer, and written information is available on request. Here is the card.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: The salad is not safe for me, so I will choose a sealed bottle of water instead.

turns.speaker: Cook
turns.text: Of course. Here is the sealed water.

blocks.title: Scene 3: The Bill in London
paragraphs: This is a fictional sit-down café beside a food market in London, Britain. The practice bill says “discretionary service charge.” In Britain, bills may use two different labels: discretionary service charge or compulsory service charge.
Your goal is to identify the charge, ask whether another tip is needed, and complete the payment.

images.alt: An adult traveller points to a café bill while a server holds a card terminal beside a London food market.

blocks.title: Roleplay: Check the Bill in London

turns.speaker: Server
turns.text: Here is your bill.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Thank you. Is this service charge discretionary or compulsory?

turns.speaker: Server
turns.text: For this practice bill, it is discretionary, not compulsory.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Is it already included, and do I need to leave another tip?

turns.speaker: Server
turns.text: Yes, the discretionary charge is already on this bill. You do not need to add another tip in this exercise.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I understand. I will keep the charge and pay by card.

turns.speaker: Server
turns.text: Thank you. Your payment is complete.

blocks.title: Your Turn: Choose the Right Words
blocks.intro: Speak through each situation. Change one detail and try again.

items.prompt: You want fruit by weight, but you do not know whether the stall takes cards. What do you say?
items.explanation:
Half a kilo of ...

Order the amount, then ask about card payment before the seller prepares it.

items.prompt: You have an allergy and want a ready-to-eat dish. What three questions or statements do you use?
items.explanation:
What is in ...?

State the allergy, ask about the ingredient, and request written allergen information.

items.prompt: A restaurant bill includes a service charge. What do you ask before adding more money?
items.explanation:
Is this service charge ...?

Check whether the charge is included and whether another tip is needed.

blocks.title: Final Reflection
blocks.intro: Choose the useful rule you most want to remember.

items.prompt: Which market question will be most useful on your next trip, and why?
items.explanation: Choose one phrase and explain the situation where you will use it.

items.prompt: What will you check before you leave a tip in another country?
items.explanation: Think about counter or table service, the bill, and the local custom.

rows.meaning: A small place where a seller offers goods in a market.
Sold according to how heavy something is.
rows.example: The cheese is sold by weight.

rows.meaning: Something that can cause an allergic reaction.
rows.example: Ask the seller about each allergen.

rows.meaning: When a small amount of one food touches another food.
Money added to a bill for service.
rows.example: The bill includes a service charge.
